paras: The threatened lynching in Indianapolis took place in April 1903, when a crowd of white men sought to kill an unnamed Black man in Indianapolis, Indiana, and the city police called out an alarm to stop them. No death was reported, and the incident survives only in brief comments in Southern white papers, which cited it as proof that lynching was not confined to the South.

According to a paragraph credited to the Washington Post, the Indianapolis police were "compelled to turn in a riot alarm the other day to save the life of a negro a crowd of white men wanted to kill." Because that paragraph had already been reprinted in a South Carolina weekly dated April 22, the incident occurred on or before about April 20, 1903. The Columbus Commercial of Mississippi gave a slightly different version, saying the police had to turn in a "general fire alarm" to prevent "a crowd of infuriated white men" from lynching the man. The Grenada Sentinel likewise wrote that the police turned on a general fire alarm "to prevent a mob from lynching a negro."
None of the reports names the man, gives the reason for the crowd's anger, or says where in the city the crowd gathered.
No report of arrests, charges, or any later proceedings appears in the coverage, and none says what became of the man.

The story traveled through the Southern white press in two textual forms between April 22 and May 6, 1903. The Washington Post paragraph ran in the Batesburg Advocate among its "Wireless Telegraph Items" and then in the Manning Times and the Marlboro Democrat, closing with the remark that "such little incidents" showed "the geographical ramifications of the race problem." The Columbus Commercial added its own sarcastic comment, "Negro-lynching is one of the enjoyable pastimes that does not belong exclusively to the South," and the Okolona Messenger reprinted that paragraph on May 6.

In the Commercial the item sat among other editorial paragraphs, including a joke that Mississippi had lynched no one lately only because people were too busy with politics. The Grenada Sentinel, by contrast, printed a bare one-sentence brief between notes on anti-Jewish riots in Bessarabia and a Black man said to have survived a legal hanging in Alabama. All the located reports appeared in white Southern papers that used the Northern incident to make a sectional point; no Indiana or Black-press account of the alarm was found.
The accounts differ on the kind of alarm, which the Washington Post called a "riot alarm" and the Mississippi papers a "general fire alarm," and none of them was written from Indianapolis.

reader.title: Threatened lynching in Indianapolis (April 1903)
bases: A crowd of white men sought to lynch or kill a Black man and police called out an alarm to prevent it (A1, A2, A5); no killing is reported, so it is a threatened lynching.

The reports describe a crowd or mob prevented by police from lynching a Black man (A1, A2, A5); none reports that he was killed, and no accusation or motive is given, so this was a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

The Washington Post paragraph (A1) and the Columbus Commercial paragraph (A2) agree on the core event in differently worded accounts, with a third version in the Grenada Sentinel (A5); all are brief second-hand comments, and no local Indianapolis dispatch was found.

framing.detail: The Washington Post, as reprinted in South Carolina, called it one of 'such little incidents' showing 'the geographical ramifications of the race problem', a sectional point rather than a condemnation of the crowd.

The Columbus Commercial wrote that 'Negro-lynching is one of the enjoyable pastimes that does not belong exclusively to the South', a sarcastic sectional retort placed beside a quip that Mississippi had not lynched anyone lately only because people were busy with politics.
The Grenada Sentinel gave a bare one-sentence news brief among other short items.
